title: Trading, swapping and swarming
blurb: Use trading (swapping) to absorb change without growing scope, and swarming to clear a blocker before escalating it.
question: A new requirement arrives mid-iteration, and separately a developer is stuck on a task she cannot solve alone. Which issues technique fits each situation?

teach.h: Two team-level techniques of the issues practice
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile gives teams two techniques for dealing with issues without calling in the board. Trading, also called swapping, handles emerging change by replacing one or more requirements, features or stories with others of a similar size in effort. Swarming is when the whole team focuses together on a stuck task, a problem or a blocker. One absorbs change; the other clears obstacles.

teach.h: Trading: like for like, agreed with the PO
teach.body: Instead of piling a new requirement on top of existing work, the team trades out a lower-priority item for it. The key to success is that only items of similar effort are swapped, and that the change fits the project's overall goals. To do this well, the team needs strong communication with the product owner, who agrees the priority of both the new and the existing items. The workload stays balanced and the current iteration is not disrupted.

teach.h: Swarming: many hands on one blocker
teach.body: Swarming can be used in several ways, for example to finish a task faster or to meet a time-sensitive need. It is especially effective for resolving issues: when a story is stuck, or an obstacle arises that one team member cannot solve alone, the team swarms on it together. Because the team owns its work, it tries swarming first, and escalates the issue to the project manager only if the team cannot resolve it.

Team coach Hannah Price's team is building an online reservation service. Mid-iteration, users ask for an email reminder: a detail change. With product owner Femi Adebayo, the team agrees it outranks a 'print history' story of similar effort, so they trade them. Two days later, developer Priya Shah cannot get the catalogue search to return results. The team swarms on it that afternoon and fixes it, so nothing needs escalating to project manager Neil Hart.

teach.text: Trading is NOT a way to clear a blocker, and swarming is NOT a way to absorb new requirements. And trading works inside the baseline: a change that alters the project backlog needs a formal decision, not a swap.

items: Trading (swapping): replace items with others of similar effort to handle emerging change (11.4.1).
Trading keeps overall scope the same and does not disrupt the current iteration.
Agree the priority of new and existing items with the product owner.
Swarming: the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker; also speeds time-critical work (11.4.2).
Swarm first; escalate to the PM only if the team cannot resolve it.

summary: You can now use trading to absorb a new requirement without growing scope, agreeing priorities with the product owner. You can also use swarming to clear a blocker as a team before escalating it to the project manager.

A.q: What is trading, or swapping, in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Moving a developer between teams to clear a blocker
Replacing requirements with others of similar effort
Exchanging time tolerance for extra scope tolerance
Passing a story from one iteration to the next release
A.why: Trading handles emerging change by replacing one or more requirements, features or stories with others of a similar size in effort (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Clearing a blocker is swarming, and it does not involve moving people between teams.
whyNot.2: Time has zero tolerance by default; trading swaps items, not tolerances.
whyNot.3: Carrying work over is not trading; trading swaps one item for another of similar effort.

options: Splitting a large epic into many small stories
Adding extra people from other projects to a team
The whole team focusing together on a stuck task
Releasing several increments at the same time
A.why: Swarming is when the team focuses together on a stuck task, problem or blocker; it can also speed up time-critical work (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Splitting epics into stories is backlog refinement, not swarming.
whyNot.1: Swarming uses the existing team, not extra people from elsewhere.
whyNot.3: Release timing is part of release planning, not swarming.

A.q: When trading items, with whom should the team agree the priority of the new and existing items?
options: The product owner
The project executive
The agile coach
Project assurance
A.why: Effective trading needs strong communication with the product owner to assess and agree the priority of both new and existing tasks (11.4.1).

whyNot.1: The executive is accountable for the project; team-level priorities sit with the PO.
whyNot.2: The agile coach works on organization-level adoption, not item priorities.
whyNot.3: Project assurance monitors governance and principles; it does not set backlog priorities.

B.q: A developer hits a problem with a story's acceptance criteria that she cannot resolve alone. Which technique should the team use first?
options: Trading the story for another
Raising an exception report
Swarming on the problem
Reassessing the Agilometer
B.why: Swarming is particularly effective for resolving a problem or blocker that one team member cannot solve alone (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Trading handles emerging change; it is not used to resolve blockers.
whyNot.1: An exception report is for a forecast breach of tolerance, not a team-level blocker.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer assesses agile-working risk; it does not solve a blocked story.

B.q: What is the key to successful trading?
options: Adding new items on top of the existing work
Asking the board to approve each swap made
Trading Must haves first because they are biggest
Swapping items of similar effort that fit the goals
B.why: The key is to swap only tasks needing a similar amount of effort, with changes that align with the project's overall goals (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Adding work on top grows scope; trading replaces items to keep the workload balanced.
whyNot.1: Trades of detail items are agreed with the PO at team level, not by the board.
whyNot.2: Must haves are fixed; lower-priority items are the ones traded out.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Trading increases the overall scope of work.
2. Swarming can speed up time-sensitive work.
3. Trading is a technique for removing blockers.
4. Trading avoids disrupting the current iteration.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Swarming can accelerate time-sensitive work (2), and trading absorbs change without disrupting the current iteration (4) (11.4.1, 11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is wrong: trading keeps overall scope unchanged.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: trading does not grow scope, and it is not used to clear blockers.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is wrong: blockers are tackled by swarming, not trading.

C.q: A team is blocked on a task. In what order should it act, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Raise an exception report, then swarm on the task
Swarm on it, then escalate to the PM if unresolved
Trade the task out, then tell the board at closure
Escalate to the board, then swarm if it agrees
C.why: The team tries swarming first and escalates the issue to the project manager only if it cannot resolve it (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: An exception report is for a forecast tolerance breach; the team swarms before escalating anything.
whyNot.2: Trading is not a blocker technique, and closure is far too late to report it.
whyNot.3: Blockers are first tackled by the team; the board is not the first step.

C.q: Mid-iteration, the PO agrees that a new detail requirement outranks an existing story of similar effort. Which technique applies, and what happens to overall scope?
options: Trading; overall scope stays the same
Swarming; scope grows to fit the new item
Swarming; scope stays the same
Trading; scope grows by one story
C.why: Trading swaps the lower-priority story for the new one of similar effort, so overall scope does not increase (11.4.1).

whyNot.1: Swarming tackles blockers, and adding without swapping would grow scope.
whyNot.2: Scope stays the same here, but the technique is trading, not swarming.
whyNot.3: It is trading, but trading replaces an item, so scope does not grow.

C.q: A change would add a new Must have epic to the agreed project backlog. Can the team trade it in, and why?
options: Yes, because trading keeps the overall scope of work the same
Yes, because the product owner agrees every priority change
No, because it alters the baseline and needs a formal decision
No, because trading is a technique for removing blockers
C.why: A new Must have that alters the agreed project backlog is a baseline change, handled formally by the board or change authority, not traded at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Trading does keep scope level, but it applies to detail changes inside the baseline.
whyNot.1: The product owner agrees team-level priorities, not changes to the project backlog.
whyNot.3: Trading is a change technique, not a blocker technique; the real reason is the baseline effect.

reteach.title: The packed suitcase and the stuck zip
reteach.question: How do trading and swarming work like packing for a trip?

blocks.body: Your suitcase is full and you want to add a jumper. You take out a jacket of about the same bulk: that is trading. The case stays the same size and you agree with whoever is paying the excess baggage, the product owner. Then the zip jams. Everyone in the house gathers round to free it: that is swarming. Only if nobody can fix it do you ask someone outside for help.

blocks.text: New requirement inside the baseline = trade (with the PO). Stuck work = swarm (then escalate if still stuck).

explain.body: Trading or swapping replaces one or more requirements with others of similar effort, so new priorities fit without growing scope or disrupting the iteration.

test.q: What does trading allow a team to do?
options: Adapt to new priorities without increasing overall scope
Extend the current iteration to fit in the new requirement
Bypass the product owner for urgent requirements
Move unfinished work into the next stage plan
test.why: Trading lets the team adapt to new priorities without increasing overall scope or disrupting the current iteration (11.4.1).

whyNot.1: Timeboxes are fixed; trading swaps items instead of extending time.
whyNot.2: Trading depends on agreeing priorities with the product owner.
whyNot.3: Trading swaps items of similar effort; it is not about carrying work over.

explain.body: Swap items of similar effort that fit the project's goals, and agree the priority of new and existing items with the product owner.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. When trading, the team should agree the priority of new and existing items with the [?].
options: project manager
chief product owner
team coach
product owner
test.why: Effective trading needs strong communication with the PO to agree the priority of new and existing tasks (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: The PM manages the project within tolerances; item priorities in a team backlog sit with the PO.
whyNot.1: The CPO prioritizes across teams in the project backlog, not within one team's trade.
whyNot.2: The team coach facilitates and coaches but does not own item priorities.

explain.body: When a task is stuck or an obstacle arises that one person cannot solve, the team swarms on it together. It can also speed up time-sensitive work.

test.q: In which situation is swarming particularly effective?
options: When a new requirement must replace an old one
When a task is stuck and one person cannot solve it
When the board must decide on a baseline change
When the Agilometer shows a low slider reading
test.why: Swarming is particularly effective as an issue resolution technique when a task or story is stuck or an obstacle arises (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Replacing one requirement with another is trading.
whyNot.2: Baseline changes are decided formally by the board or change authority.
whyNot.3: Low Agilometer readings are tackled through risk planning, not swarming.

explain.body: The team tries swarming first. If it still cannot resolve the issue, it escalates to the project manager. An exception goes to the board only if tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

test.q: A swarm fails to fix a blocker. What should happen next?
options: The team trades the blocked story out of the iteration
The board receives an exception report from the team
The tester raises an off-specification for the task
The issue is escalated to the project manager
test.why: If the team cannot resolve an issue by swarming, it escalates it to the project manager (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Trading handles new requirements, not unresolved blockers.
whyNot.1: An exception report is needed only when a tolerance breach is forecast.
whyNot.2: An off-specification is a product missing its specification, not a blocked task.
